# Introduction

Since moving to Los Angeles for graduate school, I frequently heard people claim that "Los Angeles used to be better" because many businesses closed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Though this can most likely be said about any city throughout the world, this claim pushed me to examine how business closures-location closures change in Los Angeles. This analysis will use the "Listing of All Businesses" dataset from the Los Angeles Office of Finance, which was obtained from the City of Los Angeles Open Data Portal. This dataset contains all active and inactive registered business locations, with "active" being defined as a business whose owner has not notified the Office of Finance of a cease of operations. The dataset contains relevant variables such as location, location start and end date, council district, and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and description. The primary question I will try to answer with this dataset is: How did the number of business-location closures in Los Angeles change during the COVID-19 pandemic (March 11, 2020 - May 5,2023) compared with pre-pandemic and post-pandemic periods? A follow-up question that I will explore later is: Which industries experienced the greatest changes in closure frequency during the pandemic? Other potential follow-up questions will be addressed in the Preliminary Results section.

The time range for the pandemic was defined as March 11, 2020 to May 5, 2023 based on these references:

1.  https://www.cdc.gov/museum/timeline/covid19.html
2.  https://www.who.int/news/item/05-05-2023-statement-on-the-fifteenth-meeting-of-the-international-health-regulations-(2005)-emergency-committee-regarding-the-coronavirus-disease-(covid-19)-pandemic

# Data Preparation

The "Listing of All Businesses" dataset was obtained from the City of Los Angeles Open Data Portal and is maintained by the Los Angeles Office of Finance (https://data.lacity.org/Administration-Finance/Listing-of-All-Businesses/r4uk-afju/about_data). Because the primary question is focused on business-location closures, observations without a location end date were classified as active and excluded. Variables that are not needed to answer the primary question, such as "mailing address" and "location description" were also removed. Dates were converted into R date objects as well. Invalid dates, those whose end dates occur before their start date, were removed. According to the data dictionary, observations whose council district has "0" are out of the city, so these observations were removed.

Date-based categories were then created, with "Pre-Pandemic" referring to any location end date prior to March 11, 2020. "Pandemic" refers to any location end date between March 11, 2020 and May 5, 2023. "Post-Pandemic" refers to any location end date after May 5, 2023. Future location end dates, those that have not happened yet, were removed from the "Closures" data frame. The cutoff date for this was set as October 15, 2026, the date this dataset was downloaded. Acknowledging that the "Pre-Pandemic" category extends all the way back to 1977, a second data frame was created, "Closures_Adjusted," to answer potential follow-up questions. Here, periods were restricted to 1,151 days, which was the length of the Pandemic. "Pre-Pandemic was defined as any location end date between January 15, 2017 and March 10, 2020. "Post-Pandemic was defined as any location end date between May 6, 2023 and June 29, 2026. "Pandemic" was unchanged. For other potential follow up questions and visualizations, "Closure Month," "Closure Year," and "Closure.Month.Date" variables were created.

```{r}
# Read in data. Create Original Data Frame. Re-format dates. 
All_Businesses <- read.csv("C:/Users/nweit/Downloads/Listing_of_All_Businesses_20261015.csv")

All_Businesses$LOCATION.START.DATE <- as.Date(All_Businesses$LOCATION.START.DATE, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
All_Businesses$LOCATION.END.DATE <- as.Date(All_Businesses$LOCATION.END.DATE, format = "%m/%d/%Y")

# Create Closures Data Frame. Remove Unnecessary Variables. Invalid Dates Removed. Removed Out-of-City Businesses. Establish Cutoff End Date. Create "Period", "Closure.Month", and "Closure.Year" Variables. 
Closures <- All_Businesses[!is.na(All_Businesses$LOCATION.END.DATE),]
Closures <- Closures[,!names(Closures) %in% c("MAILING.ZIP.CODE","DBA.NAME","LOCATION.DESCRIPTION","MAILING.CITY","MAILING.ADDRESS")]

Closures <- Closures[is.na(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE) | Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE >= Closures$LOCATION.START.DATE,]

Closures <- Closures[!is.na(Closures$COUNCIL.DISTRICT) & Closures$COUNCIL.DISTRICT >= 1 & Closures$COUNCIL.DISTRICT <=15,]

Fixed_Date <- as.Date("2026-10-15")
Closures <- Closures[Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE <= Fixed_Date,]

Closures$Period <- ifelse(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE < as.Date("2020-03-11"),"Pre-Pandemic", ifelse(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE <= as.Date("2023-05-05"),"Pandemic","Post-Pandemic"))

Closures$Period <- factor(Closures$Period, levels = c("Pre-Pandemic","Pandemic","Post-Pandemic"))

Closures$Closure.Month <- format(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE, format = "%m")
Closures$Closure.Year <- format(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE, format = "%Y")
Closures$Closure.Month.Date <- as.Date(format(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE, "%Y-%m-01"))


# Create Closures_Adjusted with January 15, 2017 and June 29,2026 as the Cutoff End Dates.
Closures_Adjusted <- Closures[Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE >= as.Date("2017-01-15") & Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE <= as.Date("2026-06-29"),]
```

# Exploratory Analysis

For the Exploratory Analysis, I will be using both the "Closures" and "Closures_Adjusted" data frames. "Closures" includes all records from November 14, 1977 and October 15, 2026. "Closures_Adjusted" includes all records from January 15, 2017 and June 29, 2026. For each visualization, "Historic Data" will refer to the "Closures" data frame and "Adjusted Data" will refer to the "Closures_Adjusted" data frame.

```{r}
library(knitr)
Variable_Table <- data.frame(Variable = c("LOCATION.ACCOUNT..", "LOCATION.START.DATE", "LOCATION.END.DATE", "COUNCIL.DISTRICT", "NAICS", "PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION", "Period","Closure.Month", "Closure.Year", "Closure.Month.Date"), Description = c( "The account number of the business location", "The start date of the first business activity registered at this location", "The most recent end date of all business activities at the location", "The council district # reflects the current council district assignment for that location address", "The self-reported North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code, which is used in classifying business establishments", "Description of the primary NAICS code", "Pandemic Period", "Month of Closure", "Year of Closure", "Month and Year of Closure"))

knitr::kable(Variable_Table,col.names = c("Variable", "Description"),caption = "Key Variables and Descriptions")
```

## Explanation

The Historic Data table reveals that there were a total of 648,537 closures between November 14, 1977 and October 14, 2026, which was the latest closure at the time this data was downloaded. Given that each business location gets a unique location account, it makes sense that the number of unique location accounts matches the number of business-location closures. Businesses can register for different locations, so of the 648,537 closures, 590,840 had unique business names. 99% of the NAICS codes, industry descriptions, and locations were missing. While this won't affect the primary analysis, this may limit the analysis of follow-up question.

The Adjusted Data table reveals that there were a total of 234,761 closures between January 15, 2017 and June 29, 2026. Again, given that each business location gets a unique location account, it makes sense that the number of unique location accounts matches the number of business-location closures. Businesses can register for different locations, so of the 234,761 closures, 221,091 had unique business names. 98.7% of the NAICS codes, industry descriptions, and locations were missing. Again, this may limit follow-up question analysis.

```{r}
Yearly_Closures$Year <- as.integer(as.character(Yearly_Closures$Year))

```

## Explanation

The historic annual distribution indicates that closure data before the 2000's are relatively sparse. Prominent peaks in closures occurred in 2004, 2013, and 2017, which may warrant further investigation. As the plot states, 1977 and 2026 are incomplete years, so the number of closures they have should not be compared directly with the number of closures of complete years. 1977 begins on November 14, 1977 and 2026 ends on October 14, 2026.

The adjusted annual distribution focuses on the equal length Pre-Pandemic, Pandemic, and Post-Pandemic periods. Because the plot is showing closures by year, the periods overlap within 2020 and 2023. The prominent peak in 2017 is still present, but as noted, 2017 and 2026 are incomplete years. For this data, 2017 begins on January 15, 2017 and 2026 ends on June 29, 2026. The number of closures in these years should not be compared directly with the number of closures of complete years.

## Explanation

The historic monthly distribution shows greater variation in closures over time than the historic annual distribution. Again, data before the 2000's is relatively sparse. This distribution reveals more pronounced peaks, which may suggest that the peaks in the annual distribution come from a large amount of closures in certain months rather than the entire year. The highest peak in closures occurs in November 2004, with 41,576 closures.

The adjusted monthly distribution provides detail about month-to-month closures during the three periods. Prominent peaks occur in the Pre-Pandemic period. Compared to the other periods, monthly closures appear lower during the Pandemic period, and remain relatively low except for one peak in the Post-Pandemic period. The highest peak in closures occurs in March 2017, with 15,004 closures.

# Preliminary Results

I will not include the historic data in this section as the results should not be interpreted as a fair period-based comparison because the pre-pandemic period contains 43 years worth of data. The adjusted data will be the primary data frame used in this section. A equal length, period-based data frame is more appropriate than a large, historic data frame when it comes to answering the primary question.

## Primary Question

How did the number of business-location closures in Los Angeles change during the COVID-19 pandemic (March 11, 2020 - May 5,2023) compared with the pre-pandemic and post-pandemic periods?

```{r}
# Closures by Period (Adjusted Data)
Period_Count <- as.data.frame(table(Closures_Adjusted$Period))
names(Period_Count) <- c("Period","Closures")
Period_Count$Percentage <- round(100*Period_Count$Closures / sum(Period_Count$Closures),2)
knitr::kable(Period_Count, col.names = c("Period", "Closures", "Percentage"), caption = "Business-Location Closures by Period (Adjusted Data)")

Counts <- table(Closures_Adjusted$Period)
Pandemic_vs_Pre_Difference <- Counts["Pandemic"] - Counts["Pre-Pandemic"]
Pandemic_vs_Pre_Percent <- 100 * (Counts["Pandemic"] / Counts["Pre-Pandemic"] - 1)
Post_vs_Pandemic_Difference <-Counts["Post-Pandemic"] - Counts["Pandemic"]
Post_vs_Pandemic_Percent <- 100 * (Counts["Post-Pandemic"] / Counts["Pandemic"] - 1)

Comparison_Table <- data.frame(Comparison = c("Pre-Pandemic vs. Pandemic", "Pandemic vs. Post-Pandemic"), Earlier_Closures = c(unname(Counts["Pre-Pandemic"]), unname(Counts["Pandemic"])), Later_Closures = c(unname(Counts["Pandemic"]), unname(Counts["Post-Pandemic"])), Difference = c(unname(Pandemic_vs_Pre_Difference), unname(Post_vs_Pandemic_Difference)), Percent_Change = c(unname(Pandemic_vs_Pre_Percent), unname(Post_vs_Pandemic_Percent)))
knitr::kable(Comparison_Table, col.names = c("Comparison", "Earlier Period Closures", "Later Period Closures", "Difference", "Percent Change"), caption = paste("Change in Business-Location Closures between Periods"))

```

### Summary

To answer the primary question, I used the adjusted data table. This table splits each period into 1,151 days, allowing their business-location counts to be compared directly. 43.00% of closures occurred in the Pre-Pandemic period, 28.53% occurred during the Pandemic, and 28.47% occurred in the Post-Pandemic period. The Pandemic period had about 33.64% fewer closures than the Pre-Pandemic period. The Post-Pandemic period had about 0.24% fewer closures than the Pandemic Period. Therefore, reported closures declined substantially during the pandemic and remained relatively unchanged afterward. 

## Follow-Up Question 1

Which industries experienced the greatest changes in closure frequency during the pandemic?

Here, I will use the adjusted data frame again, however, I will remove any businesses missing the NAICS codes and industry descriptions. As revealed in the Exploratory Analysis, 98.7% of observations in the data frame are missing these variables. Taking this into account, a revised version of the question would be: Among business locations with available NAICS codes and industry descriptions, which industries experienced the largest changes in closures during the pandemic compared with the pre-pandemic and post-pandemic periods?

```{r}
Industry_Closures <- Closures_Adjusted[!is.na(Closures_Adjusted$NAICS) & trimws(as.character(Closures_Adjusted$NAICS)) !="" & !is.na(Closures_Adjusted$PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION) & trimws(as.character(Closures_Adjusted$PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION)) != "",]

Industry_Counts <- as.data.frame.matrix(xtabs(~ PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION + Period, data = Industry_Closures))
Industry_Counts$Industry <- rownames(Industry_Counts)
rownames(Industry_Counts) <- NULL

Industry_Counts$Pre_vs_Pandemic_Difference <- Industry_Counts$Pandemic - Industry_Counts$`Pre-Pandemic`

Industry_Counts$Pre_vs_Pandemic_Percent <- ifelse(Industry_Counts$`Pre-Pandemic` > 0, 100 * ( Industry_Counts$Pandemic / Industry_Counts$`Pre-Pandemic` - 1), NA)

Industry_Counts$Pandemic_vs_Post_Difference <- Industry_Counts$`Post-Pandemic` - Industry_Counts$Pandemic

Industry_Counts$Pandemic_vs_Post_Percent <- ifelse(Industry_Counts$Pandemic > 0, 100 * ( Industry_Counts$`Post-Pandemic` / Industry_Counts$Pandemic - 1), NA)

# Pre- vs Pandemic Table
Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic <- Industry_Counts[order(abs(Industry_Counts$Pre_vs_Pandemic_Difference), decreasing = TRUE),]
Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic <- head(Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic,10)
Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic <- Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic[, c("Industry","Pre-Pandemic","Pandemic","Post-Pandemic","Pre_vs_Pandemic_Difference","Pre_vs_Pandemic_Percent")]

knitr::kable(Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic, digits = 1, col.names = c("Industry", "Pre-Pandemic Closures", "Pandemic Closures", "Post-Pandemic Closures","Difference","Percent Change"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = paste("Industries with the Largest Changes in Closures from Pre-Pandemic to Pandemic"), row.names = FALSE)

# Pandemic vs Post- Table
Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post <- Industry_Counts[order(abs(Industry_Counts$Pandemic_vs_Post_Difference), decreasing = TRUE),]
Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post <- head(Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post,10)
Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post <- Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post[, c("Industry","Pre-Pandemic","Pandemic","Post-Pandemic","Pandemic_vs_Post_Difference","Pandemic_vs_Post_Percent")]

knitr::kable(Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post, digits = 1, col.names = c("Industry", "Pre-Pandemic Closures", "Pandemic Closures", "Post-Pandemic Closures","Difference","Percent Change"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = paste("Industries with the Largest Changes in Closures from Pandemic to Post-Pandemic"), row.names = FALSE)
```

### Summary

The first table displays the top 10 industries with the largest differences and percent changes between the Pre-Pandemic and Pandemic periods. The second table displays the top 10 industries with the largest differences and percent changes between the Pandemic and Post-Pandemic periods. Among business location with available industry classifications, "All other personal services" experienced the largest decrease in closures from the Pre-Pandemic period to the Pandemic, falling from 63 to 31. The same industry also had the largest increase in closures from the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic period, rising from 31 to 71. Of the 10 industries shown in the first table, they all experienced a decrease in closures between the Pre-Pandemic period and the Pandemic. Of the 10 industries shown in the second table, they all experienced an increase in closures between the Pandemic and Post-Pandemic period. As mentioned above, this data only includes the observations that had non-missing NAICS codes and industry descriptions. With 98.7% of 234,761 observations missing those variables, 231,814 observations were removed, and only 2,947 observations were retained for analysis. Therefore, the tables provide a small description of the industry closure patterns and may not represent full industry closure patterns across all of Los Angeles.

```{r period-summary, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
names(Monthly_Closures)[3] <- "Closures"

Monthly_Mean <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = mean)

Monthly_Median <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = median)

Monthly_SD <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = sd)

Monthly_Min <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = min)

Monthly_Max <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period,data = Monthly_Closures,FUN = max)

Period_Summary <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = "Period"),list(Monthly_Mean, Monthly_Median, Monthly_SD, Monthly_Min, Monthly_Max))

names(Period_Summary) <- c("Period", "Mean", "Median", "SD", "Minimum", "Maximum")

Period_Summary$Months <- as.numeric(table(Monthly_Closures$Period)[Period_Summary$Period])

Period_Summary <- Period_Summary[,c("Period", "Mean", "Median", "SD", "Minimum", "Maximum")]

knitr::kable(Period_Summary, digits = 1, col.names = c("Period", "Mean", "Median", "Standard Deviation", "Minimum", "Maximum"),caption = "Monthly Business-Location Closures by Period (Adjusted Data)")

boxplot(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, col = c("blue", "red", "green"), border = "gray", xlab = "Period", ylab = "Monthly Closures", main = "Distribuition of Monthly Closures by Period (Adjusted Data)")
```

```{r}
Monthly_Closures <- aggregate(rep(1,nrow(Closures_Adjusted)), by = list(Closure_Month = Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Month.Date), FUN = sum)
names(Monthly_Closures)[2] <- "Closures"
Largest_Month <- Monthly_Closures[Monthly_Closures$Closures == max(Monthly_Closures$Closures, na.rm = TRUE),,drop = FALSE]
Largest_Month$Month <- format(Largest_Month$Closure_Month,"%B %Y")
Largest_Month <- Largest_Month[, c("Month", "Closures")]
knitr::kable(Largest_Month, col.names = c("Closure Month", "Number of Closures"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),caption = paste("Historical Month with the Largest Number", "of Business-Location Closures"))
```
